name: Society Turn PUD
keyQuestion: Should the largest single development in San Miguel County history — 19.7 acres of housing, a medical campus, and a 125-room hotel — be evaluated for its cumulative regional impact before approval?
whyItMatters: At nearly 20 acres, Society Turn would be the largest single development in county history. The project includes 121 employee housing units, a 40,000 sq ft regional medical center, a 125-room hotel, and commercial/flex space — but the 1,058 new employees it would attract still lack an identified housing plan.

name: SMART Gondola & Measure 3A
jurisdiction: SMART (San Miguel Authority for Regional Transportation)
keyQuestion: Is the gondola capital program appropriately scoped and financed, and what is the true cost of long-term operations and debt service to regional taxpayers?
whyItMatters: SMART's gondola program carries an estimated $40M in public debt. Measure 3A was a ballot issue asking voters to authorize additional bonding. The gondola is the primary public transit link between Telluride and Mountain Village — its financing and governance affect every resident and visitor in the region.
costNote: Confirmed — $40M public bond authorization (Measure 3A); full project cost not publicly disclosed.

name: VooDoo Affordable Housing
keyQuestion: With a $23M balloon payment due around 2032, how does the Town plan to refinance or repay the VooDoo project debt — and what happens if market conditions don't cooperate?
whyItMatters: VooDoo is a 27-unit affordable housing project financed with approximately $27.4 million in public funds. A balloon payment of roughly $23 million comes due around 2032. The project demonstrates both the community's commitment to workforce housing and the fiscal risks of the financing model used.
costNote: Confirmed — $27.4M public financing per Town debt records. 27 units / $1,015,000 per unit.
balloonNote: ~$23M balloon payment due approximately 2032. The Town has not publicly disclosed a confirmed refinancing or repayment plan. If market conditions are unfavorable, the Town may need to refinance at higher rates or tap general fund reserves.

name: Chair 7 / Former Hotel Development
jurisdiction: San Miguel County Open Space District
keyQuestion: Was the Chair 7 area effectively dedicated to the Open Space District in 1979, and does a former hotel concept on that land honor or violate that public commitment?
whyItMatters: In 1979, the Chair 7 area was understood by many to be dedicated to San Miguel County's Open Space District. A subsequent hotel development concept raised questions about whether that public land commitment can be unwound decades later.

name: Four Seasons Resort and Residences Telluride
keyQuestion: The Four Seasons is housing hundreds of construction workers in Naturita, Ridgway, and the West End — communities that say they 'already operate at full capacity.' Who pays when the burdens fall down-valley but the benefits flow inward to Mountain Village?
whyItMatters: The $1 billion Four Seasons broke ground in October 2025 and is under active construction — 36 months, finishing ~2028. The approved program includes 53 hotel rooms, 38 hotel residences (sold as lock-off lodge units), 29 private condominiums, and just 10 employee apartment studios in 3,000 SF of onsite workforce housing. No total staff headcount was published in the SPUD application; the document references '24/7 Front Desk Staff' and valet services but nowhere estimates the FTE count for a full 5-star operation at this scale. For context, a comparable Four Seasons property typically runs 1–2 staff per key — suggesting 50–100+ permanent employees for the hotel rooms alone, with far more across F&B, spa, housekeeping, and residences. The 10 on-site studios are plainly insufficient. Construction has already pushed workers into Naturita (developer purchased the 42-room Rimrock Hotel), Camp V, and Ridgway, where the Town of Ridgway filed suit in March 2026 against MTN Lodge for housing workers in a commercially-zoned hotel. Norwood Mayor Candy Meehan called it 'saturation at an unprecedented level.' The developer's community benefit package included $2.2M to the Mountain Village housing fund — a notable contribution, though a fraction of the reported $580M+ in project financing.
costNote: Confirmed — $1B announced project cost per developer/media; $417.5M construction loan. 52 hotel rooms / $19,231,000 per room.
keyIssues: 53 hotel rooms + 38 hotel residences (77 lodge units) + 29 private condos
Only 10 employee apartment studios (3,000 SF) for a 5-star operation — no staff count published
394,738 SF conditioned space; 506,493 SF combined with parking/mechanical
Max height 89.8 ft (hotel) / 78.2 ft (residences) — both exceed typical MV heights
$2.2M contribution to Mountain Village housing fund (community benefit)
168 parking spaces (23 in excess of code requirement); 75% EV-capable
Construction workers housed in Naturita, Ridgway, and West End communities

name: Six Senses Telluride
keyQuestion: Six Senses houses 56 employees on-site — the most workforce housing per square foot of any hotel in North America, developers claim. But a 77-room luxury resort will employ far more than 56 people. Where do the rest live, and what does that mean for a region already at capacity?
whyItMatters: Six Senses Telluride is a $285 million, 77-room luxury resort being developed on the last large hotel site in Mountain Village, approved by Mountain Village Town Council and targeting a 2028 opening. It is the first Six Senses property in the U.S. and IHG's first luxury mountain resort in North America's Mountain West. The project dedicates 14,000–15,000 sq ft to employee housing for 56 staff — which developers describe as the most workforce housing per square foot of any hotel in North America. But a 77-room full-service luxury resort with rooftop pool, Omakase dining, speakeasy bar, spa, and 24 residences will require substantially more than 56 operational employees. Viewed alongside the Four Seasons (52 rooms, opening same year), this is 129 new luxury hotel rooms added to Mountain Village in one construction cycle — all drawing from the same regional workforce with no regional housing plan to match.
costNote: Confirmed — $285M announced project cost per developer/media. 77 hotel rooms / $3,701,000 per room.

name: Sunnyside Housing Project
keyQuestion: How does the Sunnyside project address Telluride's documented workforce housing shortage, and at what public cost per unit?
whyItMatters: The Sunnyside project is one of several housing initiatives aimed at addressing Telluride's severe shortage of workforce housing. The project's financing structure and unit count will affect how many workers can afford to live in town rather than commuting 25+ miles daily.

name: Carhenge Lot Redevelopment
location: SW Telluride — surface parking lot near Lift 7

upcomingHearings.description: Consideration of an application for a Work Session on proposed new construction on Town property, pursuant to LUC 5-201.C

keyQuestion: The Town of Telluride is proposing to redevelop the Carhenge parking lot — Town-owned land at the base of Lift 7 — into a mixed-use housing and commercial neighborhood. What is the cost, who benefits, and what say does the public have before it's built?
whyItMatters: The Carhenge site (Lots 34 and 34B) is a Town-owned surface parking lot in southwest Telluride. The Town and Design Workshop are advancing a concept for mixed-use housing, underground parking, and community-serving commercial uses through a full entitlement gauntlet: HARC design review, PUD, Subdivision, and Large Scale Activity applications. As of May 2026 the project is in HARC work session review, with a broader public hearing process ahead. This is one of the last large, Town-owned development sites in Telluride proper.
costNote: Estimate — based on Canyonlands/Tower House comparable ($867/SF all-in ex-land) applied to 213,400 SF above-grade program (sum of Buildings A–F per Exhibit C site plan), plus 230 underground parking spaces × $60,000/space. Town-owned land ($0 acquisition). 230 units / $864,000 per unit.

name: Norwood / Wright's Mesa Housing & Infrastructure
jurisdiction: Town of Norwood / San Miguel County
keyQuestion: Are housing and infrastructure investments in Norwood and Wright's Mesa keeping pace with population pressures from Telluride-area workers priced out of the east end?
whyItMatters: Norwood and Wright's Mesa serve as the agricultural and working-class heart of San Miguel County. Workers priced out of Telluride increasingly commute from this area — 25+ miles each way. Housing and infrastructure decisions here shape whether down-valley communities remain economically viable.

name: Nucla / Naturita / West End Economic Development
jurisdiction: San Miguel County / Town of Nucla / Town of Naturita
keyQuestion: As the West End transitions away from coal and uranium extraction, what public investments and civic infrastructure are being planned to support economic diversification and long-term community stability?
whyItMatters: The Nucla-Naturita corridor represents the West End of San Miguel County — a community in economic transition after the decline of extraction industries. Major civic and infrastructure decisions in this area will determine whether these communities stabilize or decline, affecting the county's fiscal balance and regional identity.

name: Canyonlands / Tower House Affordable Housing
location: West Telluride — near Clark's Market, Colorado Ave corridor

documents.title: Canyonlands / Tower House Community Presentation — June 2023

keyQuestion: The Town of Telluride acquired two parcels near Clark's Market (Tower House in 2018, Canyonlands in 2021) specifically for affordable housing. What will be built, at what cost, and who will it serve?
whyItMatters: These two Town-owned parcels — 0.33 AC Tower House and 0.20 AC Canyonlands — represent some of the last infill land in west Telluride purchased specifically for affordable housing. The 2023 program called for 35–45 units, ~85% deed-restricted at 80–150% AMI, with a mix of rental and for-sale units. Construction is now underway (basement level as of May 2026).
costNote: Estimate — $3M land + $26M construction loan + $4.7M soft costs (18%) + $1.4M water/sewer tap fee waivers (~35 taps × $40K). 40 units / $877,000 per unit.

name: Shandoka Lot L — Parking Garage & Affordable Housing
location: Southwest Telluride — near Lift 7 / San Miguel River
description: Redevelopment of 4.07-acre Town-owned Shandoka Lot L into a structured parking garage with ~900 public commuter/skier spaces, ~60 affordable housing units (57,600 SF), ~6,000 SF neighborhood-serving commercial (childcare, food bank, fitness), and a 2,700 SF transit center. Project requires a PUD due to site coverage, height, and floor area variances. High groundwater and San Miguel River proximity are key site constraints. P&Z Work Session filed May 2026 by Design Workshop on behalf of the Town.
keyIssues: ~900 public parking spaces — intercept/commuter strategy to reduce town traffic
~60 affordable housing units (57,600 SF); limited free-market units allowed
~6,000 SF neighborhood-serving commercial: childcare, food bank, fitness
PUD required for height, site coverage, and floor area variances
High groundwater and San Miguel River corridor constraints
Replaces existing gravel lot; connects to Lift 7 and River Trail
costNote: No official estimate released (May 2026). Housing est. based on comparable Telluride deed-restricted projects ($700K–$900K/unit). Parking est. based on structured garage comps in mountain resort towns ($45K–$65K/space); below-grade portions will run higher. No public funding plan identified.
applicant: Design Workshop (on behalf of Town of Telluride)
keyQuestion: Can the Town afford to build ~900 public parking spaces AND 60 affordable housing units on a flood-constrained lot — and who pays for it?
whyItMatters: Shandoka Lot L is a publicly owned site at the edge of the San Miguel River corridor, and this is the Town’s most ambitious housing + infrastructure project in a generation. Alternative 2 packs a 900-space structured garage, 60 deed-restricted units, childcare, and neighborhood commercial into 4 acres — requiring height, site-coverage, and floor-area variances from Town code. No official cost estimate has been released, but comparable projects suggest a $90M+ price tag with no identified funding source. Community objections focus on: the scale and massing of the garage structure in a residential neighborhood; whether public money should subsidize intercept/skier parking rather than local commuter needs; the high groundwater and San Miguel River floodplain constraints that will substantially increase construction costs; and whether bundling housing with a parking structure is the most cost-effective path to affordable units. HARC and P&Z review begins May 2026.

name: Diamond Ridge — Community Housing
location: West of Telluride — Last Dollar Rd turnoff, Hwy 145
jurisdiction: Town of Telluride / San Miguel County (joint)
description: 39-acre parcel jointly purchased by the Town of Telluride and San Miguel County in 2021 for $7.21M (50/50 ARPA funds + County reserves) to develop up to 250 single-family and duplex Community Housing (CH-zoned) units. Located near the Last Dollar Rd turnoff from Hwy 145, approximately 2 miles west of downtown Telluride. Only about 20 of the 39 acres are considered buildable given terrain and open space requirements. At least 50% of homes must be priced at or below 120% AMI; no apartments. A $5M DOLA grant awarded in 2022 was reallocated in November 2023 after litigation-caused delays. The underlying rezoning has been reversed by a district court; the project remains stalled.
keyIssues: 250 single-family and duplex homes on ~20 buildable acres of a 39-acre parcel
At least 50% priced at or below 120% AMI; no apartments
Joint public ownership: Town of Telluride (50%) + San Miguel County (50%)
June 2022 BOCC rezoning to Community Housing (CH) challenged by Deep Creek landowners
December 2022 District Court reversed BOCC rezoning — commissioner recusal issue + master plan inconsistency
$5M DOLA affordable housing grant reallocated November 2023 due to litigation delay
Land acquisition ($7.21M) already spent; no construction cost estimate or financing plan published
Project stalled pending resolution of rezoning challenge
costNote: Land acquisition: $7.21M (50% Town of Telluride ARPA funds + 50% County reserves). Infrastructure and construction costs not yet determined. $5M DOLA grant (awarded 2022) was reallocated in Nov 2023 due to litigation delay — this grant has been lost.
applicant: Town of Telluride / San Miguel County
owner: Town of Telluride / San Miguel County (joint)
decisionBody: San Miguel County BOCC / Town Council (joint)
keyQuestion: With the rezoning reversed, the DOLA grant gone, and $7.21M in public acquisition costs already on the books — what does it actually cost to build 250 homes on a mesa six miles from town, who finances it, and does the math close?
whyItMatters: Diamond Ridge is a 39-acre parcel the Town of Telluride and San Miguel County bought jointly in 2021 for $7.21M — half from Town ARPA funds, half from County reserves — to build up to 250 single-family and duplex Community Housing units near the Last Dollar Rd turnoff. The county rezoned the land to Community Housing (CH) in June 2022, but neighboring Deep Creek landowners challenged the vote on procedural grounds: they argued a participating BOCC commissioner had a conflict of interest and that the rezoning was inconsistent with the San Miguel County Master Plan. In December 2022 the District Court reversed the rezoning. The practical fallout was swift — a $5M DOLA affordable-housing grant was reallocated in November 2023 when the litigation-caused delays pushed the project past the grant's timeline. As of 2026 the land sits vacant, the rezoning is unresolved, and neither the Town nor the County has published a construction cost estimate or a financing plan for the homes themselves. Supporters argue the project is essential to house workers priced out of the local market. Opponents have questioned both the procedural basis of the original rezoning and whether placing 250 homes on this particular parcel — on a mesa with limited road access and significant terrain constraints — is the right use of scarce public capital. The $7.21M is already spent. Whatever comes next will cost considerably more, and no one has yet said where that money comes from.

name: Society Turn — Medical Center
keyQuestion: The Society Turn PUD reserves a 40,000 sq ft medical campus site — when will construction drawings be submitted, and who will operate the facility?
whyItMatters: The PUD for Society Turn was approved with a 40,000 sq ft regional medical center as a centerpiece of the program. As of 2026, no construction drawings have been submitted. The site is entitled but unbuilt — raising questions about whether the medical facility was a condition of approval or an aspirational use. San Miguel County has long lacked adequate local medical infrastructure, making the timeline and operator commitment significant public interest questions.
costNote: PUD approved; no construction drawings submitted
